relationship: Repaired landmarks on the dedication route
rationale: The Sheep Gate and Tower of Ananeel named in the priests' repair section occur again on the later procession's route; this identifies shared named landmarks without reconstructing unmentioned distances.
The Fish Gate repaired here is a named landmark passed by the later wall-dedication procession.

Although their adoreem do not undertake service in the first repair notice, the Thekoin are later credited with a second section. The additional work is attributed to the group, not to a change of heart by those who refused.

relationship: Isana gate on the procession route
rationale: The gate of Isana repaired here appears as the gate of the isana along the later dedication route; the wording is retained without silently replacing it with a different gate name.

relationship: Broad Wall in repair and dedication
rationale: Both notices explicitly name the Broad Wall as a limit along the wall, first in the work account and later in the procession route.
The Tower of the Thannourim in the repair account corresponds to the tower of the thennourim in the dedication route; the differing forms are retained and no measurements are inferred.
The Valley Gate is named in the earlier night inspection and again in its rebuilding notice; the link does not silently identify every differently named gate in the inspection account.

relationship: Dung Gate in the inspection route
rationale: The Dung Gate reached during the earlier inspection is the gate whose repair, covering, doors and bars are described here.

Both passages name the steps of the City of David on the wall route, once in the repair description and once in the dedication procession. The Pool of Fleeces is not thereby identified as the King's Pool from another passage.

relationship: David's tomb as a surviving landmark
rationale: The repair boundary refers to the garden of David's tomb, while Peter later points to David's still-existing tomb. The comparison concerns the named royal burial, not a claim that Acts supplies the wall's precise location or garden boundaries.
Both descriptions locate the Water Gate toward the east along the wall route; the later procession does not independently identify the Nathinim's entire residential area.

relationship: Second section despite earlier nonparticipation; same-chapter
rationale: The Thekoin's second repair section follows an earlier notice that their group worked while the adoreem declined service; no later participation by those particular refusers is invented.

relationship: Sheep Gate closes the repair circuit; same-chapter
rationale: The repair list begins with priests building the Sheep Gate and ends with metalworkers and merchants working in the intervening space at its ascent; the tradesmen are not substituted for the earlier priestly builders.
Sanaballat's anger and laughter at the wall work continue the earlier mockery involving him, Tobia and Gesam after the rebuilding proposal.

Nehemiah asks that the mockers' reproach return on their own heads; the psalm likewise asks repayment of the neighbours' insult. The targets of the petitions differ, and no direct quotation is claimed.
The request not to cover lawlessness resembles Jeremiah's explicit request that the Lord not acquit his enemies' injustices or erase their sins, within a prayer concerning their murderous counsel.

The enemies react with displeasure when the breaches begin to close, but later respond with fear and recognition of God's work when the wall is completed; the different stages and reactions are preserved.
The opponents gather to attack Jerusalem, but their counsel is exposed and scattered, allowing the people to return to their wall work.

Praying while posting guards combines dependence on God with a city watch, the two matters held together in the psalm's statement that a watchman labours in vain unless the Lord guards the city; this is a comparison, not an asserted quotation.

relationship: Secret attack defeated by disclosure; same-chapter
rationale: The enemies intend to arrive unseen, kill and stop the work; the later notice says their plan became known, God scattered their counsel, and work resumed.

relationship: Warning makes the threat known; same-chapter
rationale: The neighbours' warning about attackers approaching from every place is followed by the enemies learning that their plan had become known, after which the builders return to work.

relationship: Battle exhortation grounded in God's help
rationale: Nehemiah urges the people not to fear and to remember God as they prepare to fight; the law's battle address likewise forbids fear because the Lord goes with His people to fight and save them.

relationship: Work resumes after the hidden plot fails; same-chapter
rationale: Returning each person to the work reverses the enemies' stated aim of an unseen murderous attack that would stop the building.
The arrangement dividing the people between work and armed support is later described as continuing through the day, with half holding spears from dawn until stars appear.

Those carrying loads work with one hand and hold a dart with the other, while the builders have swords at their waists. The paired descriptions give different defensive arrangements rather than the same weapon posture for everyone.

relationship: Purpose of the horn explained; same-chapter
rationale: The notice of the horn-sounder beside the builders is explained by the order to gather wherever the horn is heard during a threat.

relationship: Dispersed workforce receives a rally signal; same-chapter
rationale: The explanation that the great work leaves people far apart directly leads to the horn signal telling them where to gather.

The assurance that God will wage war for the gathered defenders corresponds to the law's promise that He goes with the people to fight their enemies; it does not identify these defensive preparations with an earlier battle.

relationship: Daily continuation of the armed work plan; same-chapter
rationale: The account of half the people holding spears throughout the daylight period continues the previously stated division between workers and armed support.

relationship: Watch duty organized through day and night; same-chapter
rationale: Requiring overnight lodging in Jerusalem for night watch and daytime work makes practical the earlier posting of guards by day and night; it does not remove the earlier emphasis on prayer.
The people's and wives' outcry against fellow Jews is explained by the complaint that their children face slavery and their land has passed to the honored men.
The need to obtain grain so families can eat and live corresponds to the law's requirement to support a brother whose means have failed, so that he may live alongside the community.

relationship: Pledged property to be restored; same-chapter
rationale: The complaint that fields, vineyards and houses must be pledged for food is answered by Nehemiah's demand that those specifically named properties be restored.

relationship: Impoverished kin must not be treated as slaves
rationale: The protest over fellow Jews' sons and daughters being enslaved can be compared with the law protecting an impoverished brother sold within the community from household-slave treatment, including provision for his children.

relationship: Demands against a poor brother rebuked
rationale: Nehemiah rebukes each leader's demands against his brother, matching the law's prohibition on pressing a poor brother hard or charging him interest on a silver loan; no unstated interest rate is supplied.

Nehemiah contrasts the community's buying back Jews sold to the nations with renewed sales by fellow Jews; the law expressly provides for kin to redeem an impoverished brother sold to a resident foreigner.

relationship: Fear of God in economic dealings
rationale: Nehemiah calls for fear of God while ending oppressive exactions; Leviticus couples fear of God with taking no interest or increase from the impoverished brother.
Nehemiah acknowledges loans of silver and grain and calls for relinquishing the exaction; Exodus permits a silver loan to a poor brother while forbidding pressure and interest.

relationship: Restoration addresses the property complaint; same-chapter
rationale: The command to restore fields, vineyards and houses answers the earlier report that those possessions were being pledged to obtain grain; the additional olive trees and produce remain part of the fuller order.

relationship: Promise sworn and carried out; same-chapter
rationale: The leaders promise to return the property and are put under oath; the following ceremony imposes a sanction on failure and states that the people carried out the commitment.

relationship: Assembly assents to a performance curse
rationale: The assembly's Amen to the curse against failing to keep the promise resembles the law's communal So be it to a curse against failing to perform its words. The particular garment-shaking sign and economic pledge are not claimed as details of Deuteronomy's ceremony.

relationship: Twelve-year governorship and return to court
rationale: The stated period from Arthasastha's twentieth to thirty-second year corresponds to the later notice that Nehemiah went back to the king in the thirty-second year; the later narrative also explains his absence from Jerusalem.

Nehemiah contrasts his restraint with earlier governors' burdens on the people; Samuel similarly gives a public account of taking no property, oppressive gain or payment from those he led. The offices and historical occasions differ.

relationship: Refusal of coerced provisions explained; same-chapter
rationale: The statement that Nehemiah did not demand coerced bread because the people's service was heavy explains the earlier report that he and his brothers did not eat the governor's coerced provision.

relationship: Prayer to remember service for good
rationale: Nehemiah's appeal that God remember his work for the people recurs in his prayer that God remember his kindness in the house of God; the repeated memoir prayer concerns distinct reforms.
The notice that the wall was built but gate doors were not yet set is followed by the express report that the doors were installed once the wall was built.
The invitation to meet in Ono, whose harmful intent is disclosed by the narrator, receives Nehemiah's refusal to interrupt the rebuilding work.

relationship: Refusal protects the work from the invitation; same-chapter
rationale: Nehemiah's answer that he cannot come down without stopping work responds to the proposed meeting in Ono, which the preceding notice identifies as an attempt to harm him.

Sanaballat's letter presents the wall as evidence of revolt, resembling the earlier accusation to Arthasastha that Jerusalem's rebuilt walls would enable a rebellious city to withhold taxes; the two letters are distinct.

relationship: Accused and actual hiring of prophets contrasted; same-chapter
rationale: The letter accuses Nehemiah of appointing prophets for a royal claim, but the later narrative identifies Tobia and Sanaballat as sponsors of a frightening prophetic message. Their specific messages and supposed purposes differ.
Nehemiah's answer that the story was invented directly rejects the letter's charges of revolt, kingship and appointed prophets.

relationship: Opposition seeks to weaken builders' hands
rationale: The declared plan that the builders' hands should slacken and work cease resembles the earlier opposition weakening Judah's hands during temple work; the temple and wall campaigns are distinct.

relationship: Protective advice exposed as a trap; same-chapter
rationale: The advice to hide in God's house with closed doors is later identified as an unsent prophecy intended to frighten Nehemiah into sin and disrepute; the precise sanctuary space is not supplied beyond the source wording.

Nehemiah recognizes that God has not sent the speaker; Jeremiah likewise condemns prophets who speak without being sent or receiving God's word. The comparison concerns the stated lack of commission, not identity of the prophets.

relationship: Intended result of the refuge proposal; same-chapter
rationale: The stated aim of making Nehemiah afraid, sinful and discredited explains why the apparently protective proposal to enter the house and close its doors was a trap.

The prayer that God remember opponents' deeds has a later counterpart in the request to remember priestly and covenant offenses; Sanaballat is named in the surrounding marriage notice there, but the offenses are not treated as the same act.

relationship: Completed work defeats the stated aim; same-chapter
rationale: The exact notice of completion after fifty-two days reverses the enemies' stated aim that frightened, slackened hands would prevent completion.

relationship: Fear replaces displeasure at the work
rationale: The nations' fear and recognition of God's completion contrast with the opponents' earlier displeasure as the breaches began to close; completion changes their response.

relationship: Letters used for information and intimidation; same-chapter
rationale: The exchange of letters between Tobia and Judah's honored men provides the channel later described as carrying the parties' words and sending letters to frighten Nehemiah.

Tobia's marriage and oath connections with leading Judeans can be compared with the later priestly favour that gives him a temple treasury room. The priest's closeness is not identified as either marriage named here.

relationship: Purpose of the correspondence disclosed; same-chapter
rationale: The reporting of each side's words and Tobia's frightening letters explain the previously mentioned traffic between Tobia and Judah's honored men.
Installing the doors after the wall answers the earlier qualification that, although the wall was built, the gate doors had not yet been set.

Both passages give orders for shutting the gates and stationing guards, but the first regulates daily security and the later order keeps burdens out during the Sabbath; their schedules and purposes are not conflated.
The notice that the large city has few people supplies the problem addressed by the later lot selecting one in ten to live in Jerusalem and praise for volunteers who settle there.
The book Nehemiah finds concerns the first returnees; Ezra's register likewise opens with those returned from Babylon and the leaders accompanying Zorobabel.
Both register introductions describe return from the deportation imposed by Nabouchodonosor and resettlement of each person in his own town.
Both registers begin with Zorobabel and include Neemias, Mardochaios and Baana, but have different additional names and name forms; the entries are not equated person by person.
Both return registers list Phoros with 2172; the family name and count agree.
Both registers list Saphatia with 372, preserving the same named household and total.
Both name Era, but Ezra gives 775 and Nehemiah 652; the parallel entry is retained with the numerical difference.
Both list Phaathmoab and the Iesoue/Jesus and Ioab/Joab grouping, but the totals are 2812 in Ezra and 2818 in Nehemiah; the source name forms and figures remain distinct.
Both registers list Ailam with 1254, an exact name-and-count correspondence.
Both list Zathoua, with 945 in Ezra and 845 in Nehemiah; neither total is corrected to match the other.
Both registers give Zakchou a total of 760.
Both registers name Banoui, but the recorded totals differ, 642 in Ezra and 648 in Nehemiah.

The parallel family-list section has Babi with 623 in Ezra and Bebi with 628 in Nehemiah. The differing spelling and count are preserved as record variants, without claiming that spelling alone proves family identity.
Both registers name Asgad, but Ezra records 3222 and Nehemiah 2322; the thousand-person difference is preserved.
The parallel entries read Adonikam with 666 in Ezra and Adenikam with 667 in Nehemiah; both the spelling and total differ and are left as written.
Both registers list Bagoi, with 2056 in Ezra and 2067 in Nehemiah.
The parallel section lists Adin with 454 in Ezra and Edin with 655 in Nehemiah; the two names and totals are compared as written, not reconciled into one numerical claim.
Both entries identify Ater in relation to Ezekia and give 98, a correspondence in both the identifying phrase and count.
Nehemiah places Baithleem with 123 and Netopha with 56 in one actual unit, while Ezra gives Bethlehem 123 and Netopha 56 in two separate units; the place form and source-unit boundaries are retained.
Both registers list Anathoth with 128.
The corresponding locality entries are Asmoth and Bethasmoth, each with 42; the added place-name element is retained rather than silently removed.
Both registers group Kariathiarim, Kaphira and Beroth together and give 743.
Both registers group Arama and Gabaa together and give 621.
The parallel locality entries read Machmas and Machemas, each with 122; the source spellings remain as printed.
Both name Bethel and Aia together, but Ezra gives 423 and Nehemiah 123.
The corresponding locality section gives Nabou and Nabi-aar, each with 52; this is a comparison of the register entries, not proof from the shared number alone that every name element is identical.
Elam-ar in Ezra and Elam-aar in Nehemiah each have 1254 in the corresponding part of the locality list; the spelling distinction is retained.
Both registers give Eram 320 in the locality section, distinct from the later priestly entry with a similar name.
Both registers give Jericho 345; its position relative to the Lod group differs.
Both group Lod and Ono with a third locality, but that middle name is Aroth in Ezra and Adid in Nehemiah, and the totals are 725 and 721.
Both name Sanaa, with 3630 in Ezra and 3930 in Nehemiah.
Both priestly sections begin with a house associated with Iesous/Jesus and a count of 973, but the head name is Iedoua in Ezra and Jodae in Nehemiah; the wording is not normalized.
Both priestly lists give Emmer 1052.
Both priestly lists give Phassour 1247.
The corresponding priestly entries read Erem with 1007 in Ezra and Eram with 1017 in Nehemiah; both name form and count differ, and this is not confused with the locality Eram entry.
Both Levitical entries give 74 and include Iesous/Jesus, Kadmiel and Odouia/Oudouia; the different wording of their relationships is preserved rather than made into a single exact genealogy.
Both identify the singers as sons of Asaph, but give 128 in Ezra and 148 in Nehemiah.
Both gatekeeper lists share Saloum, Ater, Telmon, Akoub and Atita; the last name is Sabaou versus Sabi, and the totals are 139 versus 138.
Both begin the Nathinim section with a three-name group ending in Tabaoth; Ezra has Souia and Asouphe, while Nehemiah has Sea and Asipha, preserving their differing forms.
The next groups both end in Phadon, with Keraos and Soea in Ezra and Kiras and Souia in Nehemiah; the comparison rests on the parallel register section, not a forced identification of every spelling.
Both sections contain Labano/Labana and Agaba, but Ezra's third name is Akaboth while Nehemiah's is Salami. Those two names are not equated.

Nehemiah groups Labana, Agaba and Salami; the adjacent Ezra units have Labano and Agaba, then Akaboth, Agab and Samalai before Anan. The additional Ezra names are preserved, and Akaboth is not simply equated with Salami.
Nehemiah groups Anan, Gadel and Gaar; Ezra has Anan at the end of one unit and Kedel and Gaer in the next. The group crosses a different unit boundary and the name forms are retained.
Nehemiah's Raaia, Rason and Nekoda correspond to the section with Reea followed by Rason and Nekoda across two Ezra units; Raaia and Reea are compared as written without adding a biography.
Nehemiah lists Gezam, Ozi and Phese where the adjacent Ezra units have Gazem, Ousa and Phase. These are compared within the parallel sequence with their distinct spellings.
Nehemiah has Besi, Meinom and Nephosasim; the comparable Ezra section has Basi, then Asena, Maonim and Naphison. Ezra's additional Asena is not identified as a replacement for another name.
Both groups include Bakbouk and Arour, with Akipha in Ezra and Achipha in Nehemiah; the same three-entry pattern is retained with its spelling difference.
Both groups begin with Basaloth, but continue with Maouda and Aresa in Ezra versus Meida and Adasan in Nehemiah; the varying names are not silently replaced.
Both registers give the same three names in this group: Barkous, Sisara and Thema.

The closing Nathinim pair is Nasoue and Atoupha in Ezra, Nisia and Atipha in Nehemiah; the parallel section is compared without asserting that the differing spellings themselves prove individual identity.

Ezra's next section is labelled sons of Abdeselma and lists Sati, Asepherath and Phadoura; Nehemiah labels its corresponding section sons of Salomon's slaves and lists Souti, Sapharath and Pherida. The labels and names are preserved separately.
The parallel three-name groups are Ieela, Darkon and Gedel in Ezra and Jeale, Dorkon and Gadel in Nehemiah; this is a register comparison, not an added biographical identification.
Both groups begin with Saphatia and continue with Atil/Etil and Emi/Emim, but Ezra has the combined form Phacherath-aseboin where Nehemiah separately lists Phacharath and Sabaim.
Both registers give 392 for the combined Nathinim and following servant-family groups, despite the differing Abdeselma and Salomon's-slaves section labels.
Both lists introduce returnees unable to prove Israelite descent, naming Thelmeleth and Charoub among their origins; the other place forms differ and remain as written.
Both list Dalaia, Tobia and Nekoda among those with unverified descent, but Ezra also includes Boua and gives 652, while Nehemiah gives 642.
Both priestly lists describe a Berzellai/Berzelli name acquired through marriage into the Galaadite family; the other names and the singular wife/plural wives wording differ.
Both accounts state that the missing genealogical record led to exclusion from the priesthood on grounds of descent.
Both have Athersatha prohibit eating the holiest food until a priest can provide divine illumination; Ezra adds the perfect things, while Nehemiah says the priest will give light.
Both registers give the whole assembly as 42360; this agreement does not silently reconcile differences in the component entries.
Both give 7337 male and female slaves, but the additional male and female singers number 200 in Ezra and 245 in Nehemiah.
Both inventories record 736 horses and 245 mules.
Both inventories record 435 camels and 6720 donkeys.

Both accounts record gifts for the work after the return register. Nehemiah gives a contribution of 1000 gold pieces, 50 bowls and 30 priestly chothonoth to Neemia; Ezra gives different aggregate amounts and labels, which are not harmonized with this contribution.
The 20000 in gold and 2200 silver minas from some family heads differ from Ezra's 61000 gold minas and 5000 silver minas for the work; neither the units nor the allocation are silently equated.

Nehemiah separately reports gifts from the remaining people, including 67 priestly chothonoth, while Ezra introduces leaders' gifts and reports 100 priestly kothonoi in its inventory. The donor groups, name forms and totals remain distinct.
Both register endings place priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants and the people in their towns; Nehemiah adds the arrival of the seventh month.

Nehemiah's transition states that the seventh month arrived with Israel in its towns; Ezra uses the same setting before the people gather in Jerusalem. The assemblies that follow are not asserted to be one identical occasion.
